Open Policy Analysis for:

California Proposition 40, Reconciliation of the Two Analyses

Proposition 40, the Billionaire Tax Act, would tax Californians worth $1 billion or more once, at 5% of their net worth, payable over five years. The BSZ analysis (Boll, Saez and Zucman, NBER, August 2026) finds that it raises about {{bsz_printed}} of wealth tax. The JR analysis (Jaros and Rauh, NBER, September 2026) finds that it leaves the state about {{nber_npv_round}} poorer (their paper prints an average of {{nber_printed}}), because billionaires who leave stop paying California income tax for ever. This page puts both on one definition and shows which assumptions make the difference. It follows the Open Policy Analysis (OPA) framework: the result, the method and the materials each have their own page, and every input is marked by the kind of evidence behind it.

BSZ main estimate1 {{hl_bsz}} Net total: the wealth tax, plus income tax from assets sold to pay it, minus income tax lost to leavers over 5 years, in today's dollars
JR main estimate1 {{hl_rjkdc}} Net present value: the wealth tax minus the income tax lost for ever, in today's dollars. It is the exact average of the authors' model. Jaros and Rauh (September 2026) print {{nber_printed}}, the average of one simulation of 100,000 random draws.

Today's dollars (present value): what income tax lost in future years is worth now. Both analyses count the wealth tax at face value. The Act lets it be paid in five yearly installments, each later one with a deferral charge of 7.5% a year on the unpaid balance, which neither analysis counts.

How AI was used in this exercise, and what has been verified #

who did what, and what a person has checked

This work was a collaboration between the author and Claude Code (Opus and Sonnet models) across many sessions, not an AI working alone. The table records who led the work on each public object of the comparison, using the CRediT contributor roles. The author gave these answers in a questionnaire on 2026-10-15, all 14 roles and the verification question for each object; they were not inferred from commit history. The table groups the 14 roles into three: ideas and direction (conceptualization, methodology, supervision, project administration), doing the work (data curation, formal analysis, investigation, software, validation, visualization) and writing (original draft, review and editing). Funding does not apply. Resources (computing and analysis tools) are not in the table. Claude led them for the explorer and this page, and they do not apply to the other objects. Each square in a cell is one role, coloured by who led it (key below the table). The last column is not part of CRediT. It records how closely the author has checked the object. The role-by-role answers are in CREDIT.md.

Human verification: not reviewed lightly reviewed reviewed

Human verification uses three levels: not reviewed, lightly reviewed (checked, but the author cannot yet explain it clearly) and reviewed (the author can explain it to others). The automated test suites are mechanical checks, not an outside review. No other person has verified this work, and the original authors have not reviewed it.

This OPA and the Hoopes comparison #

the one published comparison, and what this OPA adds

Jeffrey Hoopes (SSRN 6428578, 2026) is the one published comparison of the two estimates. It compares earlier versions: the February 2026 GGSS expert report (Galle, Gamage, Saez and Shanske), on which the BSZ analysis builds, and the March 2026 JR analysis. Its Figure 2 prints no values and comes with no code or data, so its steps cannot be recomputed. This OPA uses the latest versions, publishes the code, and bridges the two estimates step by step (a sequence of steps from one main estimate to the other, one input at a time). The report sets his bars beside this bridge, difference by difference.

{{quantity_survey_mini}} {{quantity_table_root}} {{quantity_survey_root}}

Kinds: data (settled by observable facts), research (a published estimate), guesswork (asserted without data or a study behind it), guesswork on data (a judgement applied to observed facts), scenario (a choice of which world is estimated) and derived (computed from the analysis's own inputs: the JR discount rate is the one rate worth the same as the authors' random draw of it). A source ending in .R is a script in the authors' repository.

1 The number each analysis's overview page leads with, out of the many settings each analysis can be run at. The BSZ number is this OPA's net total over 5 years at 3%: the {{bsz_row1}} wealth tax (Table 5 row 1), plus income tax from asset sales, minus income tax lost to leavers. BSZ's own headline is the wealth tax alone. The JR number is the authors' mean net present value in perpetuity. {{jr_fn_root}} The report gives the details.
